title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
Udio built an AI music generation system trained on recorded music and deployed it publicly without first obtaining licenses from the rights holders whose recordings were used. The core failure is straightforward: a system was trained on copyrighted material and released commercially before the legal basis for that training was established. The dispute did not concern an edge case or an unexpected use, but the foundational act of ingesting protected recordings to build the model.

Universal Music Group settled and reached a licensing agreement with Udio, and Warner Music Group did the same, resulting in a planned platform that would use only authorized music. Sony Music filed a separate new lawsuit alleging that more than 30,000 of its recordings were copied for training, and a court allowed a class action brought by independent artists to proceed, moving it from Illinois to New York rather than dismissing it. What this shows is that settling with some rights holders does not resolve exposure to others, and that the volume of allegedly copied material, tens of thousands of individual recordings, made the scope of the problem unusually large.

None of the lawsuits described here have produced final verdicts, and the allegations against Udio, including the specific figure of 30,000 copied recordings, remain claims rather than established facts. Whether Udio's outputs were substantially similar to existing works in a legally actionable way, and whether the training itself constituted infringement, are questions the ongoing litigation has not yet resolved.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio by reaching licensing agreements. The dispute centered on Udio's use of copyrighted music to train its artificial intelligence system, which generates original songs from text prompts. UMG and other major record labels had accused Udio of creating songs similar to existing hits, such as The Temptations' "My Girl," without permission or compensation. UMG's CEO stated the settlement demonstrates the company's commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technologies.

Under the settlement, Udio has agreed to launch a new platform next year using only authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize and share compositions. The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. Udio said artists can opt into the platform and receive compensation, though specific details remain unclear. This represents Udio's first major licensing agreement with a record label. The company also announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.
